extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and naturalists interested in evolution, sexual selection, and animal aesthetics (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and interpret behavioural, sensory, morphological, and ecological evidence that birds possess aesthetic sensibilities and that sexual selection has produced ornamental characters. The page gives criteria and examples—taste for scent, music, color, form, symmetry, nest/bower-building, ornament definiteness, and their relation to mate choice and fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure derived from sweet tastes and fragrant perfumes
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pleasure derived from sweet tastes and fragrant perfumes is so purely sensuous that nobody doubts its universal existence among all the higher animals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of gustatory and olfactory attraction (preference for sweet foods, fragrant fruits/flowers, scent-glands) is treated as clear evidence of a sensuous aesthetic faculty. Examples: fruits frequented by birds; scent used in sexual selection. Use as baseline evidence that higher animals experience sensuous pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondness for musical sounds (preference for pure tones)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is quite impossible to doubt that birds are fond of musical sounds... a large majority of these presumably sexual calls ... are true musical sounds, not mere noises."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral responses to music (singing-matches, mimicry, enunciated intervals), ability to distinguish harmonic intervals, and reactions to instruments (canary, starling, mocking-bird, piping bullfinch) count as evidence. Note also analogies to insects and humans; look for imitation, interval recognition, and increased song when exposed to music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for pure/simple analytic colors over confused mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Most animals preferring the relatively pure and simple analytic colors, red, blue, green, and yellow, to confused mixtures such as brown, gray, and mud-color."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecological patterning (bright hues in fruits that depend on birds; prevalence of bright plumage in flower-feeding and fruit-eating species) supports this preference. Use occurrence of bright, analytic colors in species and in their food sources as indicators of color-based aesthetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attraction to brilliancy and shiny objects
rubrics_metrics.description: "Birds certainly share ... the common fascination for bright lights ... Magpies delight in secreting diamonds, gold, silver, and other shiny objects. The bower-birds use shells, polished pebbles, and like brilliant odds and ends in the construction of their bowers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct observations of birds collecting/arranging shiny materials, approaching lamps/mirrors, and incorporating reflective objects into bowers/nests indicate a sensibility for brilliancy. Use as behavioral evidence of aesthetic attraction to light/shine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of color and delicate gradation of tints
rubrics_metrics.description: "Much of the beauty of birds, as of insects, fruits, and flowers, is due to the delicate gradation of tints ... [natural products] produce gradual merging of tint in tint ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plumage and surrounding environment for harmonious color schemes and subtle gradations rather than crude, discordant juxtapositions. The ubiquity of graduated tints in natural ornaments (versus crude human manufacture) is cited as evidence of evolved aesthetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility to form, symmetry, and arrangement of patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lastly, we arrive at the sensibility to form, symmetry, arrangement of patterns, and the like higher sensuous aesthetic feelings... The nests of weaver-birds and many other species, as well as the bowers of the bower-birds, display a considerable taste for orderly arrangement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for symmetrical nest/bower construction, patterned ornamentation, and displays (flight, perching arrangements, dancing-like antics). Repeated, deliberate arrangement and symmetry in built structures or display postures serve as evidence of appreciation for form and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness and non-functional nature of ornamental structures as hallmark of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "They are almost always... apparently devoid of any functional use whatsoever, unless that use be the attraction of the opposite sex. They are also marked by the extreme definiteness of their shape, color, or sculpture... This combination of great specific distinctness with little apparent functional value appears to me the genuine hall-mark of organs due to sexual selection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structures are highly specific/definite in form or color but lack clear survival function (e.g., peacock train, lappets, antlers used decoratively), interpret them as likely products of sexual selection. Use absence of obvious utility plus species-specific distinctness as diagnostic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral displays analogous to dancing and art as evidence of aesthetic sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "The flight of birds in play, the antics of many humming-birds, the strange eddyings and aerial evolutions of several other species, all approach very nearly to our own idea of dancing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of elaborate, seemingly purposive motor displays (play flight, choreographed perching, singing contests) count as manifestations of higher sensuous aesthetic feeling. Treat complex, repeatable display behaviors as indicative of selection for aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherited, species-specific tastes that guide mate choice
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty relatively to the particular species... must be largely due to special inherited tastes, doubtless ingrained and physically registered in the nervous system, leading the animal to derive pleasure from the typically healthy and normal form of the opposite sex."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that mate choice is guided by heritable preferences (consistent species-specific attraction to certain traits) supports sexual selection via aesthetic preference. Look for fixation of tastes, recognition of conspecifics despite close similarity, and how divergent tastes either die out or give rise to new varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation but distinction between vigor (natural selection) and ornamentation (sexual selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most vigorous individuals would usually possess the most highly developed ornaments... Hence the very animals most likely to be sexually selected are also, on the average, those most likely to be naturally selected. Yet sexual selection really differs from natural selection, in that it gives a special direction to the ornamentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use covariance between overall vigor/fitness and ornament elaboration carefully: correlation does not equal sole causation. Extravagant, maladaptive, or awkward ornaments (bird-of-paradise plumage, peacock train) suggest sexual selection acting beyond mere indicators of vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological co-occurrence of bird preferences and plant signals (fruits/flowers)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The universality of bright hues in the fruits which depend upon birds for the dispersion of their seeds clearly shows that fruit-eating species are attracted by red, blue, purple, and yellow..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-taxonomic patterns (fruit coloration aligning with bird visual preferences; flower colors aligning with pollinators) serve as ecological evidence that birds respond to color and that sensory preferences have co-evolved with plant signals. Use such co-occurrence as circumstantial support for sensory-driven selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-taxa analogies indicating a physiological basis for perceiving harmony (sound/color)
rubrics_metrics.description: "When we reflect upon the purely physical and physiological basis... there is certainly no reason why they should not be perceived by all the higher animals alike..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous sensory capabilities in insects, quadrumana, and reptiles (musicality, color preference, iridescence) bolster the claim that aesthetic responses to harmony have a physiological basis. Use comparative examples (crickets, katydids, howlers, lizards) to argue for common perceptual roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human aesthetic parallels (fitness markers) to interpret bird beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the human race we regard as beautiful... the external marks of fitness for the conditions of human life... We like in both sexes an abundant crop of hair, clear and bright eyes..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the heuristic that aspects of beauty often signal health/fitness (clear eyes, robust form) to bird morphology: plumage brightness, symmetry, and condition can be treated as indicators of individual quality. But beware of overextending human analogies without corroborating behavioral/ecological evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing limits: birds as passive selectors who may not appreciate all harmonies they produce
rubrics_metrics.description: "Man possesses the active power of direct artistic creation; the birds only possess the passive power of selection from among the forms produced for them by Nature... the birds, while selecting their partners on the ground of bright color, exceptionally long plumes... may have succeeded in producing harmonies... which they could not understand or admire."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret ornamentation and harmonies with caution: some aesthetic effects may arise incidentally from selection for simpler traits. Distinguish between traits birds actively prefer and complex emergent properties (gradations, harmonic color blends) they may not intentionally perceive.
